div.l: Or like her who, leaving her home and native land,
came to Thebes following warlike Amphitryon,
Alcmena, daughter of Electryon, rouser of the people;
she surpassed the tribe of womankind
in beauty and in stature; and in mind none vied with her
of those whom mortal women bore after lying with mortal men.
From her head and her dark eyelids
there breathed such a charm as from golden Aphrodite.
And yet she so honoured her husband in her heart
as none of womankind ever yet honoured hers;
truly he had killed her noble father, overpowering him by force,
angered about cattle; and leaving his native land
he came to Thebes as a suppliant to the shield-bearing Cadmeans.
There he dwelt in the house with his modest wife,
apart, without delightful love; nor was it allowed him
to go up into the bed of the neat-ankled daughter of Electryon
before he had avenged the murder of the great-hearted brothers
of his wife, and burned with raging fire the villages
of the heroes, the Taphians and the Teleboans.
For so it was laid upon him, and the gods were witnesses to it;
he feared their anger, and hastened as quickly as he could
to accomplish the great task which was his duty from Zeus.
With him, eager for war and battle,
went the horse-driving Boeotians, breathing above their shields,
and the Locrians who fight hand to hand, and the great-hearted Phocians,
followed; and the noble son of Alcaeus led them,
glorying in his host. But the father of men and gods
was weaving another scheme in his mind, that for gods
and for bread-eating men he might beget a defender against ruin.
So he rose from Olympus, plotting deceit deep in his heart,
longing for the love of the well-girded woman,
by night; and quickly he came to Typhaonium; and from there again
Zeus the counsellor went up to the topmost peak of Phicium.
There he sat and planned marvellous deeds in his heart:
for in that same night he lay with the neat-ankled daughter of Electryon
in bed and in love, and fulfilled his desire;
and in the same night Amphitryon, rouser of the people, the glorious hero,
having accomplished his great task, came back to his house.
He did not hasten to go to his servants and the shepherds of the fields
before he had gone up into the bed of his wife:
such desire took hold of the heart of the shepherd of the people.
And as when a man gladly escapes misery,
whether from grievous sickness or from strong bonds,
so then Amphitryon, having wound up his hard task,
gladly and lovingly came back to his home.
And all night long he lay with his modest wife,
delighting in the gifts of golden Aphrodite.
And she, subdued by a god and by a man far the best,
bore twin sons in seven-gated Thebe,
not like-minded; though they were brothers:
one a lesser man, the other a far better man,
terrible and strong, the mighty Heracles;
him she bore through the embrace of the son of Cronos, lord of dark clouds,
and the other, Iphicles, to Amphitryon the spear-wielder,
a separate offspring: the one after lying with a mortal man,
the other with Zeus son of Cronos, ruler of all the gods.
He also slew Cycnus, the great-hearted son of Ares.
For he found him in the precinct of far-shooting Apollo,
him and his father Ares, insatiable of war,
shining in their armour like the gleam of blazing fire,
standing in their chariot; and the swift horses struck the earth,
pawing it with their hooves, and the dust rose like smoke about them,
beaten up by the wrought chariots and the horses' feet.
And the well-made chariots and their rails rattled around
as the horses rushed on. And blameless Cycnus rejoiced,
hoping to slay the warlike son of Zeus and his charioteer
with the bronze and to strip off their famous armour.
But Phoebus Apollo did not hear his prayers:
for he himself stirred up the mighty Heracles against him.
And all the grove and altar of Pagasaean Apollo
shone with the armour of the dread god and with the god himself;
and his eyes flashed as with fire. Who that is mortal
would have dared to rush against him face to face
except Heracles and glorious Iolaus?
For great was their strength, and unconquerable hands
grew from their shoulders upon their sturdy limbs.
Then Heracles spoke to his charioteer, strong Iolaus:

sp.l: "O hero Iolaus, by far the dearest of all mortals,
truly against the blessed immortals who hold Olympus
Amphitryon sinned greatly when he came to well-crowned Thebe,
leaving Tiryns, the well-built city,
after killing Electryon for the sake of his broad-browed cattle;
and he came to Creon and long-robed Eniocha,
who welcomed him and gave him all fitting things,
as is right for suppliants, and honoured him more in their hearts.
And he lived exulting with the neat-ankled daughter of Electryon,
his wife; and soon, as the years rolled on, we
were born, alike neither in body nor in mind,
your father and I. From him Zeus took away his senses,
and he, leaving his own home and his own parents,
went to pay honour to the wicked Eurystheus,
wretched man! Surely he groaned much afterwards,
bearing his own folly; but it cannot be taken back.
But on me a god laid hard labours.
Friend, but quickly take the red-dyed reins
of the swift-footed horses; and raising great boldness in your heart,
drive straight on the swift chariot and the strength of the swift-footed horses,
not fearing at all the din of man-slaying Ares,
who now rages shouting round the holy grove
of Phoebus Apollo, the lord who shoots from afar;
truly, strong though he is, he shall have his fill of war."

div.l: And blameless Iolaus answered him again:

sp.l: "Good friend, truly the father of men and gods
greatly honours your head, and so does the bull-like Earth-shaker,
who holds the veil of Thebe and guards the city,
so great and strong is this mortal too
whom they bring into your hands, that you may win great glory.
But come, put on your arms of war, so that with all speed
we may bring the chariot of Ares and our own close together
and fight; for he shall not frighten the dauntless son of Zeus,
nor the son of Iphicles: rather, I think he
will flee the two sons of the blameless son of Alcaeus,
who are now close to them, longing to raise the battle-cry
of war, which to them is far dearer than a feast."

div.l: So he said; and the mighty Heracles smiled,
glad in heart, for he had said what was very fitting to him;
and answering him he spoke winged words:
"O hero Iolaus, nurtured by Zeus, no longer far off
is rough battle. As you were skilful before,
so now also wheel the great dark-maned horse Arion
about every way, and help me as you can."
So saying, he put greaves of shining orichalc,
the famous gifts of Hephaestus, about his shins;
next he put on about his breast a breastplate,
fair, golden, richly wrought, which had been given him
by Pallas Athene, the daughter of Zeus, when he was about
to set out for the first time on his grievous labours.
And he put about his shoulders the iron that keeps off ruin,
the terrible man; and about his breast he cast the hollow quiver
behind him; and within it were many arrows,
chilling, givers of death that makes speech forgotten:
in front they had death and trickled with tears;
in the middle they were smooth and very long; and behind
they were covered with the feathers of a dark-brown eagle.
And he took his strong spear, pointed with gleaming bronze,
and on his mighty head he set a well-made helmet
of adamant, cunningly wrought, fitted to the temples,
which guarded the head of godlike Heracles.
In his hands he took his shield, all glittering: no one
ever broke it with a blow or crushed it. A wonder to see!
For all round it was, with enamel and white ivory
and electrum, shimmering, and with shining gold
it was gleaming; and zones of cyanus were drawn upon it.
In the middle was Fear, of adamant, unspeakable,
staring backwards with eyes that glowed with fire.
His mouth was full of teeth in a white row,
fearful and daunting, and upon his grim brow
hovered dread Strife who arrays the throng of men:
pitiless she, who took away the mind and senses of poor wretches
who should wage war face to face against the son of Zeus.
Their souls pass beneath the earth and go down into the house of Hades;
but their bones, when the skin is rotted about them,
crumble away on the dark earth under parching Sirius.
Upon the shield Pursuit and Flight were wrought,
and Tumult, and Panic, and Slaughter blazed there.
Strife also, and Uproar were hurrying about, and deadly Fate
was there holding one man newly wounded, and another unwounded;
and another, dead, she was dragging by the feet through the tumult.
She had on her shoulders a garment red with the blood of men,
and terribly she glared and gnashed her teeth with a clashing sound.
And there were heads of dread snakes, unspeakable,
twelve of them, which used to frighten the tribes of men on earth,
whoever should wage war face to face against the son of Zeus;
and there was a clashing of their teeth whenever
the son of Amphitryon fought; and these wonderful works were ablaze.
And it was as though spots were to be seen on the dreadful snakes:
dark blue were their backs, and their jaws were black.
Also there were upon it herds of boars and of lions
glaring at each other, furious and eager:
their rows moved on together, and neither side
trembled at all, but both bristled up their necks.
For already a great lion lay between them, and about him two boars,
bereft of life, and their dark
blood was dripping down upon the ground; they, their necks thrown down,
lay dead beneath the grim lions.
And both sides were roused still more to fight because they were angry,
both of them, the bristling boars and the bright-eyed lions.
And on it was the battle of the spear-wielding Lapiths
gathered round the prince Caeneus, and Dryas and Peirithous,
Hopleus, Exadius, Phalereus, and Prolochus,
Mopsus the son of Ampyce of Titaresia, a scion of Ares,
and Theseus, the son of Aegeus, like the immortals:
they were of silver, and had armour of gold upon their bodies.
And the Centaurs were gathered against them on the other side
about great Petraeus and Asbolus the diviner,
Arctus, and Ureus, and black-haired Mimas,
and the two sons of Peuceus, Perimedes and Dryalus,
of silver, holding pine-trees of gold in their hands.
And they were rushing together as if they were alive
and striking at one another hand to hand with spears and with pines.
And on it stood the swift-footed horses of grim Ares,
made of gold, and deadly Ares the spoil-winner himself was there too,
holding a spear in his hands and urging on the foot-soldiers:
he was red with blood as if he were slaying living men,
and he stood in his chariot. Beside him stood Terror and Fear,
eager to plunge amidst the fighting men.
There, too, was the daughter of Zeus, Tritogeneia who drives the spoil,
like as if she wished to array a battle,
with a spear in her hand, and a golden helmet,
and the aegis about her shoulders. And she was going towards the awful strife.
And there was the holy company of the deathless gods: and in the midst
the son of Zeus and Leto played sweetly
on a golden lyre. There also was the abode of the gods, pure Olympus,

l.del: and their assembly, and infinite riches were spread around

div.l: in the gathering of the immortals. And the goddesses were beginning the song,
the Pierian Muses, like clear-voiced singers.
And on it was a harbour with a safe haven from the irresistible sea,
made of refined tin, wrought in a circle,
and it seemed to heave with waves. In the middle of it were many

l.del: dolphins rushing this way and that, fishing,

div.l: like swimming creatures. And two, spouting,
silver dolphins were devouring the mute fishes.
And beneath them fishes of bronze were trembling. And on the shore
sat a fisherman watching: in his hands he held
a casting net for fish, and seemed about to cast it forth.
There, too, was the son of rich-haired Danae, the horseman Perseus:
his feet did not touch the shield and yet were not far from it,
a great marvel to remark, since he was not supported anywhere;
for so did the famous Lame One fashion him with his hands
in gold. On his feet he had winged sandals,
and a black-sheathed sword hung about his shoulders
from a baldric of bronze. He was flying swift as thought.
The head of a dreadful monster covered all his back,
the Gorgon, and a pouch ran round it, a marvel to see,
of silver; and bright tassels hung down from it
of gold. And upon the temples of the lord
lay the dread cap of Hades which had the awful gloom of night.
He himself, like one who hurries and shudders with horror,
Perseus the son of Danae, was at full stretch. And after him
rushed the Gorgons, unapproachable and unspeakable,
longing to seize him. As they trod upon the pale adamant,
the shield rang with a great clatter,
sharp and shrill. Two serpents hung down at their girdles
with heads curved forward.
Their tongues were flickering, and their teeth gnashed with fury,
as they glared fiercely. And upon the awful heads
of the Gorgons great Fear was quaking. And above them
men were fighting in warlike armour,
some defending their own town and parents
from destruction, and others eager to sack it;
many lay dead, but the greater number still strove
and fought. The women on well-built towers
of bronze were crying shrilly and tearing their cheeks,
like living beings, the work of famous Hephaestus.
And the men who were elders and on whom age had laid hold
were all together outside the gates, and were holding up their hands
to the blessed gods, fearing for their own children.
But these again were engaged in battle. And behind them
the dark Fates, gnashing their white teeth,
grim-eyed, fierce, bloody, and unapproachable,
struggled for those who were falling, for they were all longing
to drink dark blood. So soon as they caught a man
lying or falling newly wounded, about him
one would cast her great claws, and his soul would go down to Hades,
to chilly Tartarus. And when they had satisfied their hearts
with human blood, they would cast that one behind them,
and rush back again into the tumult and the fray.
Clotho and Lachesis were standing over them; and the smaller one,
Atropos, was not at all a great goddess, yet she
was superior to the others and the eldest of them.
And they all made a fierce fight over one man.
They glared terribly at one another with furious eyes,
and fought equally with claws and bold hands.
By them stood Darkness of Death, mournful and fearful,
pale, shrivelled, shrunk with hunger,
swollen-kneed. Long nails tipped her hands.
Mucus flowed from her nostrils, and from her cheeks
blood dripped down to the ground. She stood leering hideously,
and much dust lay upon her shoulders,
wet with tears. Next, there was a city of men with goodly towers;
and seven gates of gold, fitted to the lintels,
guarded it. The men were making merry with festivities and dances;
some were bringing home a bride to her husband on a well-wheeled car,
while the bridal song swelled high,
and the glow of blazing torches
held by servants rolled in waves afar off. And maidens, flourishing in festal joy,
went before, and after them followed playful choirs.
The youths sang to the sound of shrill pipes
from their soft mouths, while the echo was broken around them,
and the girls led on the lovely dance to the sound of lyres.
Then again on the other side was a rout of young men revelling to the flute,
some frolicking with dance and song,
and others laughing, each with a flute-player,
went forward. Feasts and dances
and festivities filled the whole town. Others again in front of the city
were mounted on horseback and galloping. And there were ploughmen
breaking up the good soil, and they had their tunics
girt up. Also there was a deep cornfield; some were reaping
with sharp hooks the stalks which bent beneath
the weight of the ears, as if they were reaping Demeter's grain:
others were binding the sheaves with bands and spreading the threshing floor.
And some held pruning-hooks in their hands and were gathering the vintage,
while others were carrying into baskets, from the vintagers,
white and black clusters from the long rows of vines,
which were heavy with leaves and tendrils of silver.
Others again were carrying them into baskets. Beside them was a row of vines
in gold, the famous work of skilful Hephaestus:
it had shivering leaves and stakes of silver,
and was laden with grapes; and these turned black.
And some were treading out the grapes and others drawing off liquor. Others were fighting
with fists and in wrestling. Others were hunting swift hares,
men of the chase, and a pair of sharp-toothed dogs before them,
eager to catch the hares, and the hares eager to escape.
Next to them were horsemen toiling, and they contended
and laboured for a prize. Standing on well-woven cars,
the charioteers urged on their swift horses
with loose rein; and the jointed cars flew along
clattering, and the naves of the wheels shrieked loudly.
So they were engaged in an unending toil, and the victory
was never won by them, but the contest remained undecided.
And there was set out for them within the course a great tripod
of gold, the famous work of skilful Hephaestus.
And round the rim Ocean was flowing, like a swollen stream,
and enclosed all the cunningly wrought shield. Over it
swans were soaring and calling loudly, and many others
were swimming upon the surface of the water; and near them were shoals of fish.
A wonder to see, even for Zeus the loud-thunderer, by whose will
Hephaestus made the shield, great and sturdy,
fitting it with his hands. This shield the valiant son of Zeus
wielded masterfully, and leaped upon his horse-chariot
like the lightning of his father Zeus who holds the aegis,
moving lightly. And his charioteer, strong Iolaus,
standing upon the car, guided the curved chariot.
Then the goddess grey-eyed Athene came near them
and spoke winged words, encouraging them:

sp.l: "Hail, offspring of far-famed Lynceus!
Even now Zeus who reigns over the blessed gods gives you power
to slay Cycnus and to strip off his splendid armour.
Yet I will tell you something besides, mightiest of the people.
When you have robbed Cycnus of sweet life,
then leave him there and his armour also,
and you yourself watch man-slaying Ares narrowly as he attacks,
and wherever you see him uncovered below his cunningly wrought shield
with your eyes, there wound him with your sharp bronze.
Then draw back; for it is not ordained for you
to take his horses or his splendid armour."

div.l: So said the bright goddess and swiftly got up into the car
with victory and renown in her immortal hands,
in haste. Then heaven-nurtured Iolaus
called terribly to the horses, and at his cry
they swiftly drew the fleet chariot, raising dust from the plain;
for the goddess grey-eyed Athene put spirit into them
by shaking her aegis. And the earth groaned all round them.
And they came on together like fire or a whirlwind,
horse-taming Cycnus and Ares, insatiable of the war-cry.
Then their horses, facing one another,
neighed shrilly, and the echo was broken all round them.
And the mighty Heracles spoke first to that one:

sp.l: "Cycnus, good sir! Why, pray, do you set your swift horses at us,
men who are well versed in toil and distress?
But guide your well-polished car aside and yield the path
to go by. It is to Trachis I am driving on,
to Ceyx the king, who in power and in honour
stands first in Trachis, as you yourself know very well;
for you have his daughter, dark-eyed Themistinoe, to wife.
Good sir, Ares will not ward off from you the end of death,
if we two meet together in battle.
Already I say that at another time too he has made trial
of my spear, when above sandy Pylos
he stood against me, fiercely longing for battle.
Three times, stricken by my spear, he was dashed to the earth,
as his shield was pierced; and the fourth time I struck his thigh,
laying on with all my strength, and tore deep into his flesh.

div.l: And he fell headlong in the dust upon the ground through the force of my spear-thrust.
There truly he would have been disgraced among the deathless gods,
leaving his bloody spoils under my hands."
So he said. But Cycnus, the stout spearman, had no mind
to obey him and to pull up the horses that drew his chariot.
Then it was that both leaped at once from their well-woven cars to the ground,
the son of great Zeus and the son of the Lord of War.
And the charioteers drove near by their horses with beautiful manes,
and the wide earth rang with the beat of their hooves as they rushed along.
As when from the high peak of a great mountain
rocks leap forth, and fall on one another,
and many towering oaks and many pines
and long-rooted poplars are broken by them
as they whirl swiftly down until they reach the plain;
so did they fall on one another with a great shout.
And all the city of the Myrmidons, and famous Iolcus,
and Arne, and Helice, and grassy Anthea
echoed loudly at the voice of the two. And they
came together with an awful cry; and wise Zeus thundered loudly
and rained down drops of blood from heaven,
giving a sign of battle to his dauntless son.
As in the glens of a mountain a boar, hard to look upon beforehand,
a tusked one, is minded in his heart to fight
with the huntsmen, and whets his white tusk,
turning sideways, while foam about his mouth as he gnashes
drips down, and his eyes are like glowing fire,
and he bristles the hair on his mane and around his neck;
like him the son of Zeus leaped from his horse-chariot.
And when the dark-winged whirring cicada, perched on a green
shoot, begins to sing of summer to men,
the cicada whose food and drink is the tender dew,
and all day long from dawn pours forth its voice
in the most dreadful heat, when Sirius parches the skin,
then the beards grow around the millet
which men sow in summer, when the sour grapes begin to colour,
such as Dionysus gave to men, a joy and a sorrow:
at that season they fought, and a great din arose.
As two lions on either side of a slain deer
spring at one another in fury,
and there is a fearful snarling and a clashing also of teeth;
or as vultures with crooked talons and hooked beaks
fight, screaming loudly, on a high rock
over a mountain goat or a fat wild deer
which some active young man has shot and killed
with an arrow from the string, and he himself has wandered away elsewhere,
not knowing the place; but they quickly mark it,
and eagerly make a fierce fight about it;
so they two rushed upon one another with a shout.
Then Cycnus, at the son of almighty Zeus,
eager to kill him, struck his shield with a bronze spear,
but did not break the bronze; and the gift of the god protected him.
But the son of Amphitryon, the mighty Heracles,
between the helmet and the shield, with his long spear
swiftly struck his bare neck below the chin
with might; and the man-slaying ash spear cut through
both sinews; for the man's great strength fell upon him.
And he fell as an oak falls or a pine
that stands high, stricken by the lurid thunderbolt of Zeus;
so he fell, and his armour adorned with bronze clashed about him.
Then the stout-hearted son of Zeus left him there,
and himself watched for the approach of man-slaying Ares,
looking fiercely with his eyes, like a lion who has come upon a body
and full eagerly with his strong claws
rips the hide and takes away its sweet life as quickly as he can:
his dark heart is filled with fury,
and glaring fiercely with his eyes he tears up the ground with his paws,
lashing his flanks and shoulders with his tail, and no one
dares to face him and come near or fight with him:
just so, the son of Amphitryon, insatiable of the battle-cry,
stood eagerly face to face with Ares, nursing courage in his heart.
And Ares drew near him with grief in his heart;
and both sprang at one another with a cry.
As it is when a rock shoots out from a great cliff
and whirls down with long bounds, and with a roar
goes eagerly on, and a crag meets it,
a high one; with it the rock clashes, and there it holds it fast;
with no less clamour did deadly Ares, the chariot-bearer,
rush shouting at him. But he quickly received the attack.
But Athene, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus,
came to meet Ares, holding the dark aegis,
and she looked at him with an angry frown and spoke winged words to him:

sp.l: "Ares, check your fierce anger and matchless hands;
for it is not lawful for you to strip off his famous armour
after killing Heracles, the bold-hearted son of Zeus.
Come, then, cease fighting and do not withstand me."

div.l: So said she, but did not move the great-hearted spirit of Ares.
But he uttered a great shout and, waving his spears like fire,
he rushed headlong at the mighty Heracles,
eager to kill him, and hurled a bronze spear,
vehemently, angered for his dead son,
upon the great shield. But grey-eyed Athene
reached out from the car and turned aside the force of the spear.
Then bitter pain seized Ares, and he drew his keen sword
and leaped upon bold-hearted Heracles. But as he came on,
the son of Amphitryon, insatiable of fierce battle-cry,
wounded his thigh, which was laid bare under his richly wrought shield,
with might, and tore deep into his flesh
with a thrust of his spear, and threw him flat in the middle of the ground.
And Fear and Terror quickly drove his smooth-wheeled chariot and horses
near him, and lifted him from the wide-pathed earth
into his richly wrought car, and then straight away
lashed the horses and came to high Olympus.
But the son of Alcmena and glorious Iolaus,
when they had stripped the fine armour from the shoulders of Cycnus,
went their way; and straight away they came to the city of Trachis
with their swift-footed horses. And grey-eyed Athene
went to great Olympus and her father's house.
As for Cycnus, Ceyx buried him and the countless people
who lived near the cities of the glorious king,
Anthe, and the city of the Myrmidons, and famous Iolcus,
and Arne, and Helice: and many people were gathered,
doing honour to Ceyx, the friend of the blessed gods.
But Anaurus made his grave and monument vanish,
swollen with winter rain; for so Apollo,
the son of Leto, commanded it, because the famous hecatombs
that anyone brought to Pytho he would lie in wait for and violently plunder.
